html:
The Hittite kingdom was a great power of the Bronze Age in central Anatolia, today's Turkey, ruled from Hattusa from about 1650 BCE until it vanished around 1180 BCE. The Hittites spoke the oldest recorded Indo-European language, a distant relative of Greek, Latin and Sanskrit.

The kingdom was founded by Hattusili I. His grandson Mursili I marched all the way to Mesopotamia and sacked Babylon around 1595 BCE, ending the Old Babylonian kingdom. After a weak period, the kingdom rose to empire in the fourteenth century under Suppiluliuma I, who broke the rival kingdom of Mitanni and took northern Syria.

That put the Hittites face to face with Egypt:

  • In 1274 BCE the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh in Syria. Both sides claimed victory.
  • Around 1259 BCE the two powers signed a peace treaty, the oldest peace treaty whose text survives from both sides.

The Hittites wrote in cuneiform on clay, and thousands of tablets from Hattusa record treaties, prayers and the Hittite laws. A royal prayer blames a long plague on the gods' anger.

Around 1180 BCE the kingdom collapsed in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Hattusa was abandoned. Small Neo-Hittite states lived on in southern Anatolia and Syria for centuries; these are the "Hittites" of the Bible. The empire itself was forgotten until archaeologists dug up Hattusa in the twentieth century and its language was deciphered in 1915.
